issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Social Contacts' is inconsistent as written: it is phrased like a trigger ('seeing people...') rather than a strategy the patient uses. Within the Maladaptive Strategies node, the other items are clear coping behaviours, so this item is internally mismatched.

issues.item: Self-Harm Distraction: I hurt myself physically to stop thinking about the event
issues.explanation: Self-harm used specifically as a distraction is not impossible, but in this profile it stands out as clinically poorly integrated with the rest of the selected items. The other strategies are avoidance/disengagement (screen use, avoiding people), and the threat/memory profile is hypervigilance plus overwhelm. This item introduces a much more extreme coping style without supporting indicators elsewhere in the five target components, making the strategy set feel internally uneven for the same patient.

issues.item: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted
issues.explanation: For a police-related trauma in a 46-year-old civilian graphic designer, self-blame for 'the way I acted' is possible, but here it sits awkwardly beside appraisals that frame the trauma as globally ruining life and draining meaning, without any other items suggesting perceived responsibility, moral failure, or a specific behavior during the event. The appraisal set is therefore less coherent than the other nodes.

vignette: Michael, a 46-year-old European-American graphic designer, has been struggling with intrusive thoughts and overwhelming memories since an encounter with the police during which he was falsely accused of a crime. The trauma began when he was pulled over late one night for what seemed like a routine traffic stop. However, the situation escalated quickly as officers became aggressive and accusatory, eventually leading to his arrest. Michael vividly recalls feeling helpless and overwhelmed by their authority presence and the force with which they treated him. Since then, any encounter with police or even the thought of visible injuries on others immediately triggers unwanted memories and thoughts. Michael’s daily life has become increasingly difficult as these intrusive thoughts persist. They often surface when he least expects it—a sight, a sound, or simply being in a public space where authority figures are present can trigger his traumatic memory. Each time this happens, Michael finds himself unable to relax even when he knows he is safe at home. He always identifies escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere, and his body remains constantly tense, ready to react to any perceived danger. His inability to relax has deepened over the months, leading him to engage in maladaptive strategies like spending long hours on his phone or playing games to distract himself from these intrusive thoughts. These distractions help him avoid thinking about the trauma but often interfere with his work and relationships. He tries to keep his mind occupied all the time, even during social gatherings where he avoids other people because they might trigger unwanted memories. When Michael recalls the traumatic event, he feels so overwhelmed by emotion that he has to stop whatever he is doing and retreat into himself to process these feelings. Something as mundane as seeing a police officer patrolling near his office can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, causing him significant distress. This constant emotional overwhelm has left him feeling as if nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. He believes that his life has been destroyed by this trauma and that what happened to him was deeply unfair and unjust. The injustice he feels compounds his sense of threat and constantly reinforces the intrusive thoughts. His belief that his life has been irrevocably altered makes it difficult for him to trust others or feel safe in public spaces. These negative appraisals have become a part of his daily existence, intensifying each time he encounters a trigger. The memory itself is so overwhelming that Michael often finds himself trying to explain what happened but losing the thread and unable to finish his story. This inability to clearly articulate his experience further isolates him from friends and family who do not understand why these memories are so debilitating for him. The more he tries to avoid thinking about it, the more intrusive the thoughts become. Michael’s graphic design work has suffered significantly as a result of this ongoing struggle. He often misses deadlines because he cannot focus on his projects when he is preoccupied with his trauma. His wife notices that he withdraws from family activities and becomes increasingly irritable and distant. What finally brought Michael to seek help was the realization that these thoughts and memories were starting to take over his life completely, leaving him isolated and feeling like there’s no escape from his own mind. He is most afraid of never being able to reclaim a sense of normalcy or meaning in his life but also hopes for some relief from the constant emotional turmoil and the overwhelming belief that he has been irreparably damaged by this event. Through therapy, Michael hopes to find ways to manage these intrusive thoughts, learn to relax, and rebuild a sense of trust and meaning in his daily experiences.
